utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: There is one seat empty in the dock. Mr. Pusic cannot be here today; the Appeals Chamber knows why. I ask that his absence should not taken as any sign of disrespect to the Court or disrespect to any of those that have suffered because of this conflict. Mr. Pusic has made it plain in Court during this case, he said that what hit the him hardest is having to listen to the victims in this case; he finds that unbearable. He said that almost ten years ago on the 5th of October, that's transcript reference 7950. He's also asked that we, as his Defence team, make it clear that nothing we say today in the course of this appeal should be taken in any way to minimise the distress, pain, and suffering that is felt by victims of this conflict. Your Honours, today our order of submissions will be that we will begin firstly be briefly commenting on the JCE. The majority of our time will, however, be spent on directly addressing the questions that you have raised in the Scheduling Order in the order that they are contained therein, beginning with question 1, then 4, and then question 9. I am -- hope not to use all the time that's been allocated to me. I also hope that you will forgive me if I do. One of the advantages of being last on the indictment is that we can listen to what others have said and that can also be a big disadvantage in a multi-handed trial, but today I will try whenever possible to save time but adopting submission that applied to the Pusic Defence which have been already rehearsed by others. I would also encourage and invite questions from the Bench at any time. I've always found this helps focus attention on the issues that are most relevant, although I do hope that I do not come to later regret making this invitation. Your Honours, if I may begin with ground 3 of our appeal brief, which is our submission that there is no evidence of a JCE in this case. Our position remains. We say that the Trial Chamber erred in coming to a conclusion that a JCE existed. We would define the JCE in this case as a two-tier JCE. Tier 1 we refer to the ultimate goal which I will call, by way of shorthand, the Banovina reunification theory, which Your Honours will be familiar with volume 4, paragraph 24. The Banovina reunification theory we would say is a non-criminal and political aspiration. Tier 2 of the JCE, we say, is that there are the specified criminal means which are cited to achieve that goal which also form part of the JCE. Before going any further, we would just clarify what we say the law governing the JCE is, the extracts that are relevant. We accept the law allows evidence of a JCE to be inferred from circumstantial evidence. There does not have to be direct evidence of an explicit agreement. We also accept that the law allows the Trial Chamber to rely on evidence of the way in which crimes were committed as evidence of a JCE, hence the often repeated mantra relied on by the Prosecution that the best evidence that the accused is part of a common plan lies in evidence of what the accused actually did or said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Nonetheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sahota, please, if you can kindly slow down a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: What troubles us nonetheless is that the evidence that those inferences are drawn from is, we say, too ambiguous, conflicting, and contradictory to support the Chamber's conclusions, particularly when the standard of proof is so high - it's the criminal standard - and these facts have to be proved beyond reasonable doubt. The reasons we cite in support of that proposition are set out in detail in our appeal brief. I do not intend to rehearse them again here, nor do we intend to repeat all the other relevant points that the Court has already heard in relation to this submission. We would, however, like just to develop one aspect, one point, concerning the Chamber's reasoning. We say that underpinning the Trial Chamber's JCE theory is the notion that the Croatian and HVO HZ HB military and political structure was a tool or instrument in the hands of their leaders, a tool or instrument used to further a particular end, their vision of a Greater Croatia, the tier 1 of the JCE which I referred to earlier. Now I use the word "instrument" here because when reading the Trial Chamber's decision, I was reminded of the debate in political science between instrumentalists and structuralists. I should just say here that my first degree was history. The instrumentalists believe that the state is a direct instrument of the ruling class, so applying that concept to the JCE in this cases, we could say that the state and its apparatus were an instrument in the hands of Tudjman and his cohorts. He/they gave orders. What he/they wanted was executed. And it's obvious from the Trial Chamber's judgement and the indictment that Tudjman is given almost dictatorial powers in their analysis of the JCE to shape policy and events. Structuralists, on the other hand, believe that the state is not an instrument at all. They believe that the state does not exist as a thing in itself that can be bent to the will of a ruler or the ruling class; instead, it's a neutral arena. And to use a quite delightful expression from a philosopher, Nicos Poulantzas, he described the state as a neutral arena for the condensation of a balance of forces. Your Honour, this discussion is relevant to our submission because we say the Trial Chamber has erred in adopting this instrumentalist approach in formulating their JCE, in particular, tier 1 of the JCE theory. The Trial Chamber has come up with a very simple and elegant solution to a most complicated problem which boils down to this: Tudjman always wanted a Greater Croatia. When he got the opportunity to put this policy in action, he had the ability and used the state apparatus in Croatia and the HVO HZ HB apparatus as a tool or instrument to execute that policy. And the other leaders, the other accused in this case and others mensed in the JCE, agreed and went along with him. We can see that this is an elegant and superficially attractive formulation, especially when compared to the Prosecution's original contention in the indictment that there were several JCEs, not just one. However, our submission is that while this approach has the virtue of simplicity, it is it also fundamentally flawed because what this instrumentalist JCE theory can't explain is the complexities of the situation that arise when important evidence conflicts with the Trial Chamber's analysis. You've heard in the past few days many examples of what I will term inconvenient facts, facts that don't fit in with the Trial Chamber's instrumentalist analysis. I don't intend to rehearse them again, but they include evidence of Tudjman's conflictive motives. His motives seem to change and shift over time and in response to external events. Indeed, Your Honours, I said that I was a historian by training in my first degree. It is ironic when one reviews the historical literature to see how historians are divided as what Tudjman's motives are, almost in the same way the Trial Chamber was divided as to what Tudjman's motives are, contrast the minority and majority decisions, examine the lengthy narrative in the minority dissent. And, Your Honours, we say this is important because the ultimate objective of the JCE, tier 1, this must be also proved beyond a reasonable doubt. There are other inconvenient facts. Again, I don't intend to rehearse them all. Broad categories include submissions you've heard that the HVO at times was acting defensively and not pursuing an aggressive policy in terms of expanding the land mass under their control, submissions you've heard that the HVO at times or throughout did not pursue an aggressive policy of ethnic cleansing. And, Your Honours, what seems to be the case is that we say this evidence of inconvenient facts, which suggest that those named as the framers of the JCE actually had varying objectives which suggests that their modes of execution depended and changed on the dynamics of power; these inconvenient facts are largely ignored by the Trial Chamber. May I clarify here. We are not saying that there is anything necessarily wrong or incorrect with this instrumentalist JCE approach being taken in cases where an international tribunal is dealing with a large-scale conflict. But there is a very strong argument that the fever of the mind that formed the background for the Second World War and the Rwandan conflict, by way of an example, lent itself to an instrumentalist analysis. In those conflicts, in contrast to the facts that we are dealing with today, there was clear evidence of a -- of centralised control of the state. There was evidence of a clear and consistent policy agenda, suggesting a unity of purpose amongst the political actors and military actors and a narrative of conflict that suggested that one party acted aggressively. These are common threads present in those cases, not necessarily present in the more complicated factual background of the particular situation we are dealing with today in the Balkans. To put it simply, JCE theory is not an easy fit against this background. That's why deliberately in my submissions today, Your Honours, we have referred to the JCE as formulated in the majority decision as a theory, because that's what it is. It sounds great as a theory, but when you apply it to the facts it just doesn't stand up; because it's a theory that provides a factually incomplete and inaccurate characterisation of the background to the conflict; because it's a theory that's based on a highly selective reading of the evidence and a gross oversimplification of the issued raised by that evidence; and also because it's a theory that directly impacts on the reputation of the Government of Croatia, when that country has not been given the opportunity to respond to it. That's why we say that JCE as formulated is a theory that should sit alongside the many other narratives that historians and politicians and members of the public will debate in academic circles, in their parliaments, in coffeehouses for years to come. It should not and cannot stand alone as a definitive finding of fact proved beyond reasonable doubt in an international court of law. It should and cannot stand as the final word or not just what happened during the conflict and who was responsible, but also on why it happened. I ask the Chamber to pause here and consider for Your Honours to ask yourself: Was it even necessary for the Court to address and devote so much time to this question of why the conflict happened, when this is an issue that occupies historians and causes so much controversy? I remind Your Honours of what was said in Krstic, where it was re-stated that the purpose of this Court is not to set the historical record on the causes of the conflict. In Krstic the Appeals [sic] Chamber said that: "... historians and social psychologists" should be left to "plumb the depths of this episode of the Balkans conflict and to profile deep-seated causes. The task at hand is a more modest one: To find, from the evidence presented at trial, what happened ..." And, Your Honours, that's cited at footnote 182 to paragraph 104 of our trial brief. Your Honours, we say that profiling deep-seated causes is exactly what the Trial Chamber has done in this case. One cannot fail but to have those words from Krstic in mind when reading paragraphs 6 to 24 of volume 4 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. So in concluding our JCE submissions, we ask you to review the evidence cited in support of the JCE. We are confident that if you do you will find that not only was it unnecessary for the Court to consider the causes of the conflict in the detail it did, but you will find that findings it came to concerning the existence of a JCE are erroneous and unsafe. Your Honours, four years ago I addressed the Trial Chamber in my closing speech, and I said then that the Prosecution had overreached in its theory of many overlapping JCEs in the indictment. Today I submit that the Trial Chamber has overreached either further than the Prosecution did - if that is at all possible - in finding that one JCE, a grand overarching scheme, existed rather than several interlocking JCEs. Your Honours, that concludes my submissions on JCE. If I may turn now to the questions in the order that were provided by the Chamber. And if I may address each question in turn, turning to question 1 which is an inquiry into the state of occupation. Ask the Appeals Chamber at this junction to note that one of the ways in which we will be submitting in due course that the case of Mr. Pusic is different and should be distinguished from the co-accused lies in the fact that he is not actually charged in respect of any crimes that took place in Gornji Vakuf, and confirmation of this can be found at paragraphs 73 and 230 of the indictment. Thus reinforcing submissions in our appeal brief that he was not a leader or high-level official. Also apparent from the fact that he was not charged with any of the crimes that are said to have taken place in Prozor in October 1992. And it was further said in the Trial Chamber's judgement that in their opinion, he is only considered to have joined the JCE later than the others, in April 1993, the events in Gornji Vakuf having taken place some months earlier in January of that year. Your Honour, in direct response to the question raised by this Chamber at question 1, we simply adopt submissions made previously, particularly those made by the Stojic team which we don't feel that we can improve on. Moving on to the next question that directly addresses Mr. Pusic, that's question 4. Again, Your Honours, the incident in Dusa takes place in Gornji Vakuf, which is in relation to a crime that Mr. Pusic is not charged with directly. However, turning to question 4(a) there were, in our submission, be some impact on Mr. Pusic if the Appeals Chamber were to reverse their finding on Dusa; if, in turn, that finding lead to the Appeals Chamber redefining the parameters of the JCE; if a reversal of the Dusa finding lead the Appeals Chamber to reverse all the convictions for the other defendants for any crimes of wilful killing and murder that took place in the course of any attacks, on the basis that those crimes were not within the scope of the common plan; then we say that Mr. Pusic should also be acquitted of similar crime, in his case his convictions pursuant to JCE 1 for Counts 2 and 3 which are said to be wilful killings and murders that took place in the course of an attack in Mostar. So if those crimes are by implication found not to be part of the common criminal plan, then he should be also acquitted of them. Question 4(b), it follows that as Mr. Pusic was not charged with the events in Dusa, the Trial Chamber made no findings in relation to his mens rea, and we say there should be no impact on his mens rea for JCE following any reversal unless the Appeals Chamber decides to define a new legal definition of mens rea in JCE, which I frankly can't imagine is going to happen in this case. Question 4(c), Your Honours, the short answer is that we take the view that a reversal should have no impact on Mr. Pusic's acquittal for any JCE 3 crimes. We do, however, take the position that we will wait to hear what the Prosecution says in regards to this point and reserve our right to respond fully until we have heard that reply. Moving on now, Your Honours, to question 9, where the Appeals Chamber has asked for us to examine the Trial Chamber's finding that Mr. Pusic had the power to resolve problems related to conditions of confinement and the mistreatment of detainees in the network of HVO detention centres. We will focus on the Trial Chamber's findings in paragraph 1056 of volume 4, that is the paragraph cited in the footnote to question 9 in the Scheduling Order. We propose to deal with the issues raised in paragraph 1056 in this particular order: Firstly, we will look at the issue of forced labour, we will then turn to look at the question of Mr. Pusic's powers over the conditions of detention and his ability to remedy the mistreatment of detainees. So the first issue: Forced labour. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's findings -- relevant findings can be found at paragraph 1054. Mr. Pusic is said to be amongst those with the power to authorise the sending of detainees on forced labour assignments in the Heliodrom. Another relevant finding is at paragraph 1203, where it's said that Mr. Pusic played a significant role in the use of Heliodrom detainees to work on the front line, as he was one of the authorities who authorised or approved this. Your Honours, I would ask you just to note the use of the word "significant" here, contrast it with the use of the word "substantial" to describe Mr. Pusic's powers elsewhere the judgement, particularly in passages that deal with detention centres. Your Honours, we suggest - and I will elaborate on this later - that this indicates a rather muddled approach on the part of the Trial Chamber. Paragraph 1203 continues with a Trial Chamber finding that Mr. Pusic continued sending detainees to work on the front line although he knew that detainees had died and had been wounded. These allegations form, we would suggest, probably the most serious allegations that have been laid against Mr. Pusic so that we will address them in some detail. The principal evidence relied on in support of these assertions by the Trial Chamber is the evidence of one Josip Praljak. Mr. Praljak is one of the wardens at the Heliodrom. The first point that we would emphasise in relation to his testimony is that the Trial Chamber acknowledged that this witness lied on oath before an international court. The appropriate reference can be found at paragraph 1589 of volume 2. The Trial Chamber found that Mr. Praljak, Josip Praljak, lied about most important issue in his testimony, when he claimed that he had no knowledge of any detainee abuses in the Heliodrom during the time that he worked there. This was a patently absurd claim; the Trial Chamber was right to reject it. However, in our submission, the Trial Chamber did not go far enough. It should have, as a consequence, rejected his evidence in its entirety instead of cherry-picking and taking a compartmentalised approach. And what we find particularly troubling with the Trial Chamber's findings is that the Chamber accepted that Praljak was lying when it came to the issue of who was responsible or knew for what happened at the Heliodrom; but when to the same end in his testimony he pointed the finger at others, they accepted his version of events unreservedly and uncritically. And they did so without explaining why they could discard one part of his testimony but rely on another, again to make a finding beyond reasonable doubt, also suggesting that they failed to make a reasoned finding in relation to his evidence. Your Honours, it also follows that we have concerns because there is no finding made by the Trial Chamber that Josip Praljak was Mr. Pusic's subordinate and that Mr. Pusic had the authority to give him orders. And I remind the Appeals Chamber of the evidence that was heard on Friday last, when the Prosecution asserted - that's at transcript page 641 - when the Prosecution asserted its position as to who the wardens and commanders of the Heliodrom reported to and did not cite Mr. Pusic that regard. What troubles us here again is that the Trial Chamber made no finding that Mr. Pusic held any official position within the prison network. It made no finding that Mr. Pusic had any direct authority over prison governors or prison wardens or prison staff in each facility. It made no finding that he had any powers over military personnel stationed at any of the detention centres; many of those personnel were ultimately responsible for the forced label assignments, we say. It made no finding that he had any powers over the superiors of any of the officials at the prisons or to any of the military personnel stationed there. Your Honours, this point is developed at paragraphs 16 to 21 of our appeal brief. I won't repeat the submissions here, but this does go to what we've said earlier, that Mr. Pusic's case is different from the other co-accused. He is not in the cabinet. He's not a high-level political figure. There is mention in the Trial Chamber's judgement that they don't even consider him to be a high-level official. We say that it cannot be inferred from evidence of the position or any position he held that he had powers over prison staff or military commanders. That is a conclusion the Prosecution have to prove beyond reasonable doubt. And at this point we would issue a handle-with-care warning in respect of certain categories of evidence, in particular in respect of any reference by the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution to Mr. Pusic having de jure powers by virtue of any positions he held, by virtue of any position he held on the 5th of July Service for Exchange established in 1993, by virtue of any position he held or powers he had from his position that the 6th of August, 1993, commission for exchange and prisons. Your Honours, this particular organisation is the subject of several citations by the Trial Chamber, and it is puzzling to us that so much reliance is placed on evidence is connected to it when at other parts of the judgement the Trial Chamber concedes that they thought the commission was entirely ineffective. And they accept that there was no evidence it ever met. And, Your Honours, rather than rehearse this again today, I would refer to our appeals brief paragraphs 28 to 31, where we do explore this issue in more detail. Your Honours, we would also say that the Chamber should handle with care any reference to his role following the 10th of December, 1993, which is the date that Mate Boban made an order mandating that the operation of HVO detention centres should be dismantled. Our case is, quite simply, that Mr. Pusic did not have any de jure powers by virtue of any of these positions. And that is why, Your Honours, we intend to focus in the remainder of these submissions on evidence of his de facto powers. And we will continue by looking briefly at what Praljak actually said, having addressed you on his credibility. Josip Praljak gave evidence on what the Trial Chamber described as 30 -- he gave evidence of what Trial Chamber described as 30 verbal orders, each authorising the use of detainees for forced labour, and that's cited at Trial Chamber's judgement paragraph 1147 of volume 4 and also paragraph 1472 of volume 2. In summary, Josip Praljak said that he regularly received orders from the military police or military brigade officials, such as Witness NO, who was the commander of all the HVO forces in Mostar; or another witness, Pavlovic. Neither of these individuals did Mr. Pusic have any authority over. These orders were such that these military officials required detainees to be sent to the front line to perform labour assignments. The order would be passed down to the Heliodrom staff and it would be eventually handed and land on Mr. Josip Praljak's desk. Mr. Pusic at this point has no role whatsoever in this process. But for some reason when giving evidence, Josip Praljak claimed that having received this notification Mr. Pusic also had to be contacted and had to be asked to approve the use of prisoners for labour. Josip Praljak continued, he said that whoever spoke to Pusic would then have to make a note or written memorandum of their conversation and that would take the form of a note or memorandum in the Heliodrom log-book. Your Honours, in accordance with our handle-with-care warning, we would ask you to look at these orders closely. We would ask you to -- whenever you're presented with a document or order that is cited by the Prosecution or Chamber and it says that this document proves that Mr. Pusic had the power to do X, Y, or Z, we would ask you to scrutinise and look at whether the label or a conclusion applied to that document is actually justified. We would ask the Appeals Chamber to ask some basic questions. Did Mr. Pusic write or author the document or did someone else write it? And does the document really in context support the conclusions to which the Trial Chamber or Prosecution seek to draw? In relation to these 30 verbal orders, if we perform this analysis, you will find that they are documents that are not written by Mr. Pusic. They're actually notes of a conversation, and again Your Honours have heard our submissions that there is no predicate finding that Mr. Pusic had any power over Josip Praljak or the military commanders making these requests. What's also interesting is that there is a conspicuous lack of corroboration from other witnesses when they deal with this issue of who had the authority to order these forced labour assignments at the Heliodrom. No other witness who testified on this issue -- I apologise. If I do err in any way, I do obviously mean Josip Praljak. No other witness -- Josip. Thank you. No other witness who testified on this issue, and that includes Witness Pavlovic - and I apologise again if I have these pronunciations wrong, ten years at the Tribunal and I haven't improved very much but I'm trying - neither Pavlovic not Witness NO, when they gave evidence, made any reference to Pusic as a superior who had to approve these requests for forced labour assignments. And most importantly, we say, when Marjan Biskic, who was the HVO assistant minister of security, somebody parachuted in by the Croatian government towards the end of 1993 to help the Croats in BiH, if I can use the colloquial expression, to help them clean up their act. And when tasked with looking at forced labour assignments, he gave evidence at some length on the procedures that were followed at the Heliodrom. He made no mention of Mr. Pusic in his analysis. And indeed, when he was asked to comment on Mr. Pusic's authority in general, he made a comment that is at the very forefront of our submissions and not addressed at any point by the Trial Chamber he said these words. He said that: "Mr. Pusic could not give orders to me or anyone else." Your Honours, we accept and we hope the Appeals Chamber acknowledges that we are trying to be realistic here. There is evidence that could support a conclusion that Mr. Pusic was aware of what was happening in the detention centres, in that detainees were being sent out to work - sometimes on the front line - and that there were many casualties as a result of this. And in saying that, we don't necessarily concede that simply because reports were sent to him that he must have had constructive notice of their contents. But our position remains. The evidence cited by Trial Chamber, the evidentiary lied on by the Prosecution does not show that he had any authority to do anything about these forced labour assignments. And when we look at the Chamber's finding of fact that Mr. Pusic could give orders for detainees to be taken out on these assignments, when we undertake a penetrating analysis of that evidence - which we say the Trial Chamber abjectly failed to do - we are sure that you will find that no reasonable Chamber could have arrived at the conclusion that the Trial Chamber did in this instance. Your Honours, turning to the second question, conditions of detention or the second issue that arises from question 9, conditions of detention. The Trial Chamber's findings -- and in this area they refer to Mr. Pusic as having so-called substantial powers. Those findings can be found at paragraphs 1056, 1203 of volume 4. The Trial Chamber further elaborates on the evidence it relies on to support its conclusions at paragraphs 1137 to 1145 of volume 4. Their findings follow a distinctive pattern, and these are -- this is the pattern that's applied to all their findings in relation to all the detention centres in respect of Mr. Pusic. They say - the Trial Chamber says - that Mr. Pusic was aware and had the power to remedy serious problems at each detention centre, but because he omitted to do so - and he then remained in situ performing his functions - it deems his omission to act as acceptance and says that amounts to a substantial contribution to the JCE. Your Honours, in response, our starting point is that, again - and we hope the Appeals Chamber accepts that we are being realistic here - we again accept that there is evidence that could support the conclusion that Mr. Pusic was made aware of what was happening in the detention centres to some degree. So, for example, in relation to and dealing with the Heliodrom first, if you look at paragraphs 1137 through to 1141 of volume 4, we note there is material that the Trial Chamber relies on to show that Mr. Pusic may have been aware of the conditions pertaining to the Heliodrom. For example, there is the fact that he attend a meeting with the ECMM monitors on the 16th of July, 1993, at paragraph 1137 where this issue is mentioned, it's clear. There is also evidence of reports that are sent to him, and again we repeat this point about constructive motive. Just because reports are sent to you doesn't mean that it can be deemed that you have no notice of their contents. It is evidence that can't be ignored; we concede that. But we don't accept that the Trial Chamber was right in inferring that he had a power to remedy a problem simply from the evidence which suggests that he had notice or knowledge of it. We also don't accept that the Trial Chamber was correct in inferring that he had a power to remedy the problems at the Heliodrom and other detention centres from other factors that the Trial Chamber cited, including firstly the fact of his de jure authority emanating from many of the positions he held 5th of July, Service for Exchange; the 6th of August commission for exchange; powers that he had after the 10th of December. I have already addressed you in response to those findings. Secondly, we don't accept that the conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber that Mr. Pusic had powers to remedy the appalling conditions at these detention centres can be inferred from evidence that he had the authority to transfer prisoners out of one detention facility to another. This is a factor that's heavily relied on by the Trial Chamber, and they say that Mr. Pusic had the power to transfer prisoners from one facility to another, not just in respect of the Heliodrom but also other detention facilities. It's our position in response that the evidence cited by the Trial Chamber does not go to establish this. If we look just at paragraph 1144 [Realtime transcript read in error "1044"] of volume 4 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, there's reference to a report which is dated the 5th of July, 1993. This is a report -- I have been asked to correct the paragraph reference. It should actually be 1144 not 1044. Your Honours, I was referring to a report dated the 5th of July, 1993. This is a report that was sent by Josip Praljak's superior, Stanko Bozic, who was also a warden at the Heliodrom; and remember what was said by the Prosecution on Friday as to who had ultimate control over the wardens and commanders at the Heliodrom. Mr. Bozic complained that soldiers were firing at random at detainees. He in his report requested reinforcements to stop this happening again. We apply our handle-with-care warning to this document once again. When look at this closely, Your Honours, you will see that this is not an order that was written by Mr. Pusic. It was a report sent to him and not just sent to him exclusively but also circulated to others, we would suggest, who are far higher in the chain of command. There's no evidence that he ever replied. Your Honours, in a similar vein, there is another document, a report, this time that he sent, Mr. Pusic sent, on the 6th of January, 1994, that is relied on by the Trial Chamber once again to support the same conclusion that Mr. Pusic had the authority to order the transfer of prisoners between facilities. This is referred to at paragraph 1140 [sic] at volume 4. It's a report he September to Marjan Biskic asking for permission to move detainees from one facility to another. It's not an order, it's a request. If anything, it proves exactly the opposite of what the Trial Chamber tried to infer or asked us to infer. It shows that Mr. Pusic did not have the power/authority to transfer -- order the transfer the prisoners himself unilaterally from any facility. We go further than that, we also say that he did not have the power to unilaterally order the release of prisoners, and that's an additional submission that's documented at length in our appeal brief. And if I may briefly at this conjuncture just correct the last transcript reference, it should read "1142" rather than "1140." But, Your Honours, we say that in this and every case cited by the Trial Chamber, the evidence shows that whenever Mr. Pusic did anything, he had to seek the approval of higher authorities and could only act on their orders. And in this particular case, he had to seek authorisation from Mr. Biskic - a man who was never charged, a man who was presented as a Prosecution witness at his trial. We would also say something briefly about the timing of this request. The date is the 6th of January, 1994. Remember, Mate Boban's order on the 10th of December, the efforts made to dismantle detention centres thereafter. It's clear that there is evidence that Mr. Pusic attends meetings often with senior figures present, but the decision to dismantle HVO detention centres was taken by others at a much higher level than his. It's clear there is evidence that he presents reports at these meetings, but we say his interaction with the leadership, the others present, is one way that he presents reports, there's no real evidence of any feedback. Can it seriously be suggested that Mr. Pusic decided policy, made decisions at these meetings? We would say that his role is more appropriately described as that of a subordinate or clerical officer, someone charged with collating information and issuing discharge papers. Again this is a submission that's repeated at length in our appeal brief, but it's also something that has some grounding in the Trial Chamber's decision if one looks at volume 4, paragraph 1166. And we apply this analysis to evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber in December 1993 in respect of Ljubuski detention facilities that Mr. Pusic issued documents that allowed the release of detainees from that facility to third countries and also issued documents that authorised their transfer to other detention centres; and that's cited at volume 2 paragraph 2229. Your Honours, this evidence does not prove to the criminal standard that Mr. Pusic had any significant or unilateral powers to order the release or transfer of prisoners. Moving on to Dretelj. I would refer Your Honours to paragraphs 1167 to 1170 of volume 4 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. Once again, the Trial Chamber adopts the same pattern in its reasoning as evidence of Mr. Pusic's so-called powers. It cites the fact - and this is at paragraph 1167 - it cites the fact that on the 20th of July, 1993, he is appointed as part of a working group to deal with overcrowding in the various HVO detention facilities. As we state in our appeal brief, Mr. Pusic is very much the junior member of this commission. Indeed, the evidence shows that on the next day, the 21st of July, 1993, when the same commission reports back to the cabinet, he is not one of the individuals present at that meeting. And, Your Honours, this is rehearsed at paragraph 206 of our appeal brief. If we look now and turn to the Trial Chamber's findings in relation to the Gabela detention facility, paragraph 1174 at volume 4, again reference is made to Mr. Pusic's de jure powers arising from his membership of the 6th of August, 1993, commission. I won't repeat the position we take in relation to that assertion, but I would refer you to paragraph 1169. Again, the Chamber places reliance on Mr. Pusic's present membership of that commission on the 20th of September -- sorry, July -- I apologise, Your Honours. What I'm referring to is Mr. Pusic's presence at a meeting on the 20th of September where he is addressed by members of the ICRC and he is told that they have reports that detainees are suffering malnutrition at the Gabela detention facility. So as we've said before, being realistic, we accept that could be inferred as evidence that Mr. Pusic knew what was going on; doesn't necessarily mean that he had any powers to remedy those conditions. The same analysis applies if we turn to the report cited at paragraph 1175, also in relation to Gabela. This is evidence of a report that is circulated to Mr. Pusic on the 29th of September, 1993, by Ivo Kuric [phoen]. Again, it may establish knowledge; doesn't go to establish authority or power. Turning now to the Ljubuski detention facility, referring Your Honours to paragraph 1182 at volume 4. There is evidence cited by the Trial Chamber that Mr. Pusic visited this facility at least twice. The Trial Chamber goes on to say that he knew that it had limited capacity, that there was overcrowding. These matters all go to establish knowledge on his part; we concede that. But we fail to see how the Chamber can infer that he had any powers to remedy those conditions from this evidence. Again, at paragraph 1182, there is reference made by the Chamber to the -- or to evidence that suggests that Mr. Pusic ordered or could order the transfer of detainees between facilities and there are documents produced to show that this is what occurred between May and September 1993. Your Honours, we issue our handle-with-care warning again. These orders are, in fact, notes not written by Mr. Pusic but by Witness E. They are notes of orders presumably received orally by Witness E, and it says on the documents: Orders from Mr. Pusic and Mr. Koric [phoen]. Note their respective positions in the hierarchy. Note what was said on Friday. Your Honours, our submissions are further elaborated in our appeals brief; I don't intend to rehearse them here. I'm simply trying to draw your attention to these points that we have raised that we say the Trial Chamber failed to address. I know that at your leisure, once this hearing concludes, you will have the opportunity to look at them in more detail. But what we say in drawing your attention to this material is that there is no evidence that -- as the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Pusic had the power to remedy these issues and no justification for the findings that the Trial Chamber arrived at. Your Honours, in detailing with this section, our overall submission is this: We say that it has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Pusic made any significance contribution to the JCE because of the way he exercised certain powers he is said to have in respect of forced labour or because of the way he failed to exercise any powers he is said to have in respect of the conditions of detention. We say those findings are unwarranted. Your Honours, if you are with us in respect of our submissions so far, dealing with question 9, dealing with this issue of forced labour dealing with this issue of the conditionals of detention and the mistreatment of detainees and Mr. Pusic's power to remedy those problems; if you are with us, then we submit that this will have important ramifications for Mr. Pusic's conviction in general. It will have ramifications for his conviction for the other offenses on the indictment which he was also acquitted for which don't feature in the list of questions that you have provided us. Because we say that the same analysis that we have just outlined and developed applies to his so-called powers over less serious but nonetheless important aspects of the crimes he was convicted of, specifically his role in prisoner releases, his role in exchanges, humanitarian evacuations, and the allegation that he deliberately spread false information. Your Honours, once again I do not intend to repeat what is in the brief and I will be finishing very shortly. I would say that any incisive, penetrating examination of the evidence in this case will show that Mr. Pusic did not have any unilateral powers in any of these areas to issue orders. We say the Trial Chamber erred in its decision globally because they tried to compartmentalise its findings. It said that in respect of any dealings with detention centres, Mr. Pusic had substantial powers; but on the other hand it said that when looking at non-detention centre-related matters, Mr. Pusic only had significant powers. Your Honours, we suggest that what should have happened is that the Trial Chamber should have linked the evidence to do with detention centre matters and non-detention matters together. It should have linked the evidence of witnesses such as DZ and DV - and I refer you to our appeal brief - witnesses who gave evidence about their dealings with Mr. Pusic on the issues of humanitarian evacuations, prisoner releases, prisoner exchanges. What DZ and DV said is that it appeared to them that Mr. Pusic had to have the permission of his superiors to take decisions and to act. It should have linked those findings with the evidence of Mr. Biskic, who said as you will recall that Mr. Pusic could not give orders to him or to anyone else. We say the only way that you can make sense of Mr. Pusic's role is by linking this evidence, particularly as all three witnesses - DZ, DV, Biskic - were Prosecution witnesses. Your Honours, we understand the Trial Chamber's desire to make sure that those responsible for the appalling events at the Heliodrom and other detention facilities should be prosecuted and punished. We understand their revulsion when confronted with the evidence of the terrible things that happened at those centres. We saw some of that evidence on Friday. We may see more of that evidence later today. But we say even if that evidence shows that Mr. Pusic may been informed of what was happening on the ground in those centres, when it is viewed clinically and dispassionately - as it must be in any court of law - it does not prove to the criminal standard that he could have remedied those problems. And it follows from that, we say, that Mr. Pusic could not and did not make a substantial contribution to the JCE. Your Honours, I don't need to remind you that it's not for the Defence to prove anything in this case. We didn't put on a positive case at trial; that's because we took the view - and we stick to this view - the Prosecution evidence adduced did not come close to establishing Mr. Pusic's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Your Honours, I will end here with a quote from an author, Robert Caro. This quote came to mind because I've just finished his third 1.000-page volume, a monumental biography of Lyndon Johnson, which is now what I consider to be light reading, having practised here for ten years. But, Your Honour, Mr. Caro is a useful author I would suggest to refer to whenever one is called to examine the extent and ways in which political power can be wielded. There are two famous quotes attributed to Mr. Caro. First he said: "What I believe is always true about power is that power reveals." Second, he said: "You can use a biography to examine political power but only if you pick the right guy." Your Honours, we say the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber who relied on the evidence adduced at trial did not pick the right guy in this case. They picked a guy who when Slobodan Praljak was told of his name as one of the accused, he said he had to ask his secretary who he was. Who is Mr. Pusic? And, Your Honours, can you find that at transcript reference 41502 to -3. Consequently, substitute "biography" for "trial" in the quote from Mr. Caro, we say were a proper, thorough, incisive, penetrating analysis of the evidence of his role in this case reveals is not the exercise of any significant degree of power in the hands of Mr. Pusic but quite the opposite: A glaring absence of power. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that all from the Pusic -- yeah, okay. Thank you. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, there is agreement amongst the Bench. You will start and we will stop at 11.30 for a break. All right? And then continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. My colleague Ms. Bassett will be starting the Prosecution's submissions in respect of Mr. Pusic, and then she will be followed by Ms. Goy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BASSETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Marisa Bassett for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BASSETT
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Sahota has told you that Mr. Pusic is a person of little consequence. His appeal makes him out to be a clerk without significant or substantial powers, charged with collating information and processing discharge papers. This picture is misleading. Berislav Pusic was a trusted implementer of the common criminal plan. Although the Trial Chamber found - as Mr. Sahota has told you - that Pusic was not a high-ranking HVO official, it concluded in volume 4, paragraph 1093, that he was entrusted by high-ranking officials with powers that allowed him to play an important role in implementing the common criminal plan. The confidence that other JCE members placed in Mr. Pusic allowed him to take on increasingly important roles in areas central to the implementation of this plan. Pusic accepted more and more responsibility and used his powers to further the common criminal plan, volume 4, paragraphs 1202 and 1204. Between October 1992 and the summer of 1993, he rose. He rose from having occasional involvement in prisoner exchange in late 1992 and ordering prisoners to perform labour assignments in early 1993, to serving with other JCE members on commissions and delegations related to detention to - by the summer of 1993 - becoming head of the HVO's exchange service and head of the commission for HVO prisons and detention centres. It was as head of the exchange service - officially called the Service for the Exchange of Prisoners and Other Persons - that Pusic played his most important role in the JCE, strategically exchanging and releasing Bosnian Muslims held by the HVO in its network of detention centres in order to advance the HVO's objective of removing the Muslim population from the so-called Croatian provinces. Volume 4, paragraph 1202. Pusic frequently interacted with other JCE members who assigned him important tasks and appointed him to official posts. The Chamber found particularly that Pusic had regular contact with Prlic and Coric throughout his JCE membership between April 1993 and April 1994. Volume 4, paragraphs 1093 and 1221. But the Chamber's findings also show him interacting with most of the named JCE members. In April 1993, Coric appointed Pusic to participate in exchanges on behalf of the military police. As time went on, Pusic's interaction with Coric on issues related to detention became so constant that representatives of international organisations came to see Pusic as Coric's right-hand man. Pusic served alongside Petkovic on a joint ABiH-HVO delegation to Sovici and Doljani following the April 1993 attack. On the 5th of July, 1993, Prlic appointed Pusic head of the new exchange service. Later that month, Prlic also assigned Pusic to a working group to inspect detention sites in Capljina. In August 1993, Stojic appointed Pusic to head of the commission for HVO prisons and detention centres. Pusic also played a key role on the working group, implementing Mate Boban's 10th of December, 1993, decision to close the network of HVO detention centres while systematically removing the detainees from Herceg-Bosna to advance the criminal plan. Pusic also frequently reported to Prlic's government on this topic. Your Honours, all of these men trusted Pusic with roles important to the implementation of the common criminal plan, and Pusic continued to accept these positions - positions with greater and greater responsibility - demonstrating that he embraced the common plan and the means used to implement it. The Chamber's conclusion - that Pusic was a JCE member who significantly contributed to the common plan and shared the intent for the crimes forming part of it - was reasonable. My colleague Ms. Goy will address these issues and the grounds of appeal in detail in her submission. She will also answer the Chamber's questions 4(c) and 9. But before I turn the floor over to Ms. Goy, I'm going to provide an overview of the HVO's network of prisons and how it served as a vehicle to implement the common plan to remove the Muslim population from Herceg-Bosna. Your Honours have heard about this network from some of my colleagues last week already, but understanding this network is important to understanding Pusic's contributions to the common criminal plan because it is within this network that Pusic played his most important roles. He ordered prisoners to perform dangerous, unlawful forced labour. He organised prisoner exchanges and releases for the purpose of removing these persons from Herceg-Bosna. He played a key role in closing the detention centres in the network, methodically expelling detainees in this process. And he served as the link between the network and the most important JCE members. Volume 4, paragraphs 1202 to 1204 and 1209. The Chamber refers to the HVO detention centres as a "unified network," volume 4, paragraphs 980 and 982. This network included the major detention centres of Heliodrom, Ljubuski, Dretelj, Gabela, Vojno, and Vitina Otok, as well as smaller locations throughout Herceg-Bosna. Volume 4, paragraph 890 and footnote 1677. These detention centres were connected. We can see this, in particular, from the co-ordinated movements of detainees between centres, often for the purpose of eventually removing these detainees from Herceg-Bosna. There is a clear summary of the network's functioning at volume 4, paragraph 999, where the Chamber explained it as a part of a system to "expel the Muslim population." The centres were linked to the expulsions at the very heart of the JCE. The Chamber summarised: "The members of the JCE set up a system to expel the Muslim population which, more specifically, consisted of detaining civilians, holding detainees in bad detention conditions, sending some detainees to work on the front line, and removing detainees and their families from the territory of the HZ(R)HB on their release." As the JCE pursued its plan to remove the Muslims from the provinces it considered Croatian, HVO forces conducted large-scale arrested of Muslims. This included arrests also of Muslims in West Mostar. Many were detained in HVO detention centre network. By June 1993, removals became - in the Chamber's words - "more efficient," as the JCE introduced an organised system of deportation using releases from the prison network. Volume 4, paragraph 64. Across the network, terrible conditions prevailed. These conditions were calculated to coerce detainees into agreeing to leave Herceg-Bosna for ABiH-held territory or for third countries. Volume 4, paragraph 64. Facilities were overcrowded and unhygienic. Food was scarce. One detainee lost 47 kilos during his nine months of imprisonment. Heliodrom was so overcrowded that detainees had to take turns lying down. At Ljubuski there was only one toilet for up to 262 men. Prisoners were brutally treated. One was administered electric shocks while his ears were filled with water. Another had his teeth broken by a pistol that was shoved into and then pulled out of his mouth. They were humiliated. After being beaten with a pickax, a prisoner was told to lick his balija blood from the ground. Detainees were killed. Another terrifying aspect of the conditions was the use of prisoners for dangerous and unlawful forced labour. As Your Honours have heard, detainees from Heliodrom, Vojno, and Ljubuski were made to reinforce fortifications, collect HVO bodies on the front line, and serve as human shields. They were sent to mingle with HVO forces to prevent sniper fire or were dressed in uniform, given fake rifles, and placed in positions where they would draw fire. They were routinely shot and killed. Detainees faced the risk of getting one of these work assignments every day. There's powerful testimony from numerous victims in evidence. Let me tell you about one of the victims, Halid Jazvin. Jazvin was a detainee who performed labour almost every day for the four months that he was detained at the Heliodrom. One day, an HVO soldier took Jazvin and 12 others, including a prisoner named Aziz, to the front line in Mostar. Jazvin was ordered to move sandbags to build barricades. As the battle became intense, the soldier ordered Jazvin to collect wounded HVO soldiers. Jazvin said: "When we arrived outside, there was a wounded HVO soldier but about 20 metres away I noticed three or four bodies lying together in a pile. I immediately recognised one of these bodies as Aziz. I ran over to Aziz's body to see if he was alive. While I was approaching him I was shot in the leg. I crawled and I touched Aziz's body to see if he was alive. He was dead. The other two or three bodies were also prisoners." The HVO soldier, Jazvin reflected, had only cared about that wounded HVO soldier and not the lives of any of those Muslim prisoners. Your Honours, that's from Exhibit P10213, paragraph 20. These conditions and mistreatment served their intended coercive purpose. Given the option, many detainees agreed to leave their homes permanently in order to be released from detention. Of the thousands detained, many were released on the promise that they would depart for third countries via Croatia. Croatian officials helped facilitate this process by ensuring that the expelled were issued transit visas allowing a brief, temporary stay in Croatia before moving on to their final destinations. Volume 2, paragraph 1644. I also refer Your Honours to volume 4, paragraphs 1210 and 120, citing Exhibit P9679. And I further refer Your Honours to Exhibit P10048. Other detainees were released to ABiH-held territory, including to besieged East Mostar, where they continued to be terrorised. This co-ordinated expulsion process was a core aspect of the implementation of the common criminal plan. To secure a release, a detainee needed to sign a form indicating their third country destination. The detainee would be returned home, given a few hours, if any, to pack, gather their family, and then they would be taken to Croatia by bus where they were allowed to remain temporarily until they could move on to their destination state. The Chamber makes findings about these types of releases in volume 2, paragraphs 1642 to 1650 with regard to Heliodrom; as well in 1870 to 1875 for Ljubuski; and in volume 3, paragraphs 143 to 145 and 272 to 274 for Dretelj and Gabela respectfully. I also refer Your Honours, in particular, to Exhibit P9680. This expulsion process was a major part of the implementation of the common plan, so much so that Pusic referred to such deportations as "standard practice" in a proposal that he sent to Prlic in December 1993. Your Honours, this is Exhibit P7102, which can you see is a proposal from Pusic sent to Prlic personally. At page five he writes: "A recent standard practice has been that persons in possession of proper documentation (letters of guarantee, transit visas by the Republic of Croatia office for displaced persons) are released after the SIS checking and they go to third countries." The SIS, Your Honours, is the HVO's security and information service. Many who did not agree to leave or who were unable were kept in HVO's detention system and used - in the Chamber's words - "as a form of currency." Volume 4, paragraph 1121. I also direct Your Honours to Exhibit P7158 as an example. They would be exchanged to ABiH-held territory for Croats to further the HVO's efforts to alter the ethnic composition of the so-called Croatian provinces. This practice too is reflected in Pusic's proposal to Prlic. After months of effecting deportations, he tells Prlic that the exchange service is only interested in prisons "only for the purpose of seeking certain persons for exchange." JCE members used these methods - release and release through exchange - for the purpose of removal of Muslims both before and after Mate Boban issued his 10th of December, 1993, order -- decision excuse me, to close the HVO's detention centres. The evidence, however, shows that these removals began to happen at a more rapid pace from mid-December 1993. The Chamber found that Pusic had a significant role in this process. His powers increased as he took on his key role in the closure of the detention centre network, serving as a member of Boban's working group and diligently and methodically working to ensure that those leaving the facilities also left Herceg-Bosna. Volume 4, paragraphs 1050, 1203, and 1209. The last detainees in the HVO detention network were released through exchange in April 1994. Unless Your Honours have any questions, I will now turn the floor over to my colleague, Ms. Goy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Goy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will start my submissions by briefly addressing the submissions on ground 3 of Pusic's appeal on the ultimate purpose and the common criminal purpose before moving to Pusic's criminal responsibility under joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, counsel for Mr. Pusic has today challenged the Chamber's findings on the ultimate purpose and the common criminal purpose. The Chamber's findings on the JCE members' ultimate purpose have been addressed throughout last week and they are amply supported by a wealth of evidence cited in volume 4, paragraphs 6 through 24. This includes Tudjman's voluminous presidential transcripts, the evidence of those with whom Tudjman worked closely, such as Croatian Prime Minister Josip Manolic, and international representatives such as US Ambassador Peter Galbraith and Herbert Okun. Counsel for Mr. Pusic today asked whether it was necessary for the Trial Chamber to go into a lengthy discussion of the ultimate purpose. While Pusic's liability does not hinge on the ultimate purpose in the sense of the JCE members' long-term plans what to do after they had achieved ethnic domination, it was nevertheless proper for the Trial Chamber to conduct their inquiry into the ultimate purpose, as the ultimate purpose defines the overall goal that the common criminal purpose sought to achieve and therefore constitutes the relevant context for the common criminal purpose. And this common criminal purpose was amply supported by the evidence, the evidence that included the pattern of crimes; the co-ordination of the political and military leadership of Herceg-Bosna; the collaboration of this leadership with Croatian authorities; the co-operation of the accused and others to carry out criminal attacks, denials, and cover-ups; and the co-ordinated efforts to move Croats into areas claimed as Croatian; in addition to the JCE members' direct expressions of intent. And I refer Your Honours to volume 4, paragraph 51, 54, 58, 62 through 66, and 1219. I would now like to turn to Mr. Pusic's individual criminal responsibility as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. And I would like to first address Mr. Pusic's significant contributions to the common criminal plan, that is grounds 1 and 6 of his appeal, before turning to his shared intent. Before responding to the individual contributions in more detail, I would first like to address two challenges that were repeated today which are based on an erroneous understanding of the legal framework of JCE liability and, therefore, cannot undermine the Chamber's conclusion. First is that counsel today said that Pusic had no power, no authority over others, but Pusic's contributions do not hinge on his authority over others on a superior/subordinate relationship vis-à-vis the perpetrators. As I will address in a moment, Pusic had authority in areas of forced labour and prison release and this did not require that he had overall superior/subordinate relationship vis-à-vis those that actually opened the prison doors or that took the persons out for forced labour. Rather, all that was required was that Pusic had the power in relation to the use of forced labour and release, and the evidence shows that he did. Second, I would like to address Pusic's challenges based on lack of autonomous decision-making. To constitute a contribution to a JCE, the conduct does not have to be based on an autonomous decision. The jurisprudence only requires assistance in or contribution to the common criminal plan. Even the implementation of somebody else's decision can contribute to that plan. For example, in Kvocka the Appeals Chamber upheld the finding that Prcac contributed to the JCE. Prcac had some influence in his position as administrative aide at Omarska camp and contributed to the functioning of the camp and, therefore, to the common criminal purpose. That's in the Kvocka appeal judgement paragraph 622. Therefore, Pusic's arguments regarding the lack of autonomous decision-making power should be dismissed. But, Your Honours, let me now turn to the reasonableness of the Chamber's factual conclusion that Pusic made a significant contribution to the common criminal purpose. Pusic's contributions centred mainly around the network of detention facilities, a network which - as my colleague Ms. Bassett has explained - was central to the implementation of the common plan. Pusic mainly contributed to the common plan in four ways: One, by authorising the use of Muslim detainees for dangerous unlawful forced labour, including at the front line, forced labour which contributed to the horrible detention conditions that coerced the detainees into agreeing to leave Herceg-Bosna upon release; two, by using his powers over HVO detainees to remove them from Herceg-Bosna, including when implementing Boban's decision to close detention facilities; three, by being the link between the network of the detention facilities and the most important members of the JCE, such as by keeping them updated on the implementation of Boban's decision; and four, by keeping persons detained who he knew were unlawfully detained and who were held in terrible conditions and were mistreated. I will address all four contributions in turn and - in this context - will also respond to Your Honours' question number 9. The Defence challenges Pusic's power and contributions, but his powers are only relevant inasmuch as they are used or intentionally not used to further the plan. The evidence shows that Pusic did use his powers to further the plan. Pusic used his power to authorise unlawful forced labour, labour of a military nature or purpose and extremely dangerous. Volume 4, paragraphs 1054 and 1149. Forced labour was one of the means to expel the Bosnian Muslims from Herceg-Bosna. The detainees were exposed to the daily risk of being selected for highly dangerous forced labour on the front line, so dangerous that they risked being killed. And it formed part of the horrible features of the detention that the detainees could only avoid by agreeing to leave Herceg-Bosna with their families upon release. The Chamber's findings that Pusic authorised forced labour is reasonable. Although the Chamber could not pin-point to the exact source of Pusic 's power to authorise forced labour, the record is replete with evidence showing that Pusic, in fact, exercised it; that Pusic had no de jure power here is irrelevant. Importantly the Chamber noted that the term "order" and "approval" that occur in the documents are used interchangeably to refer to the step in the process that preceded the sending out of detainees for forced labour. That's volume 2, paragraph 1471. The evidence shows that Pusic approved requests for forced labour for Heliodrom detainees to build bunkers, collect bodies of fallen HVO soldiers, and to work on the front line. Volume 4, paragraph 1149. And I would like to emphasise here that the Chamber did not only rely on the evidence of Josip Praljak. Here, for example, we see a request for group of prisoners of 5 July 1993, and we can see in the left bottom corner highlighted in yellow "approved by Berko Pusic." And we know from Exhibit P2020, page 2, that Berko is Berislav Pusic. And the request says: "Please provide us a group of five prisoners for building bunkers." Exhibit P03194. A look at the military police administration log-book of requests and approvals for forced labour, Exhibit P08043, shows that in July 1993 alone Pusic approved or ordered close to 700 labour assignments. Your Honours see here the second page of the log-book and you see the line number, the subject of the work assignment, the date, and the file number, and the formation that submitted the request, and also who approved it. And we have collected from this document the lines where labour was approved by Pusic in July 1993, and this adds up to 700 individual assignments. Your Honours, I would just like to note here that we relied on the B/C/S original because the translation unfortunately contains a number of mistakes, so not all numbers reflected on our compilation are found in the translation but they are found in the B/C/S original. Detainees were also sent to perform labour on the front line pursuant to general orders of Pusic. This means that Pusic had broad powers in relation to forced labour. And I refer Your Honours to Exhibit P03583 and P03633. Contrary to the suggestions by the Defence, Marjan Biskic's testimony does not undermine the Chamber's conclusion. Biskic was deputy minister of defence for security and military police of Herceg-Bosna from December 1993, and he only arrived in Herceg-Bosna on 8 November; and therefore, his knowledge was limited to late 1993. Transcript pages 1534 and 153 -- 15034, excuse me, and 15317. And in any event, Biskic confirmed that while there was a de jure procedure and chain of command: "In practice things were somewhat different." Transcript page 15241. Biskic also added that Heliodrom Warden Bozic never refused permission to send detainees on forced labour. That's transcript page 15301 through 15302. And the evidence shows that had included times when Pusic ordered or approved the labour, Exhibit P02385 and Exhibit P03596. Therefore, the Chamber's conclusion that Pusic contributed to the common criminal purpose by authorising unlawful forced labour is reasonable, that Pusic was not the only one who authorised forced labour is without consequence. Pusic also contributed to the joint criminal enterprise by using his power over Muslim detainees to remove them from Herceg-Bosna, in particular when implementing Boban's decision to close the detention facilities. Volume 4, paragraphs 1203 and 1204. As Ms. Bassett explained, the Muslim detainees were often released under the condition that they left Herceg-Bosna, often even BiH, with their families. Volume 4, paragraph 1132. Expelling these Muslim detainees and their families was at the heart of the common criminal purpose. The evidence shows that Pusic was involved in these expulsions, such as from the Heliodrom, Gabela, and Ljubuski prison. To find that Pusic had the power and did organise and approve releases as of May 1993, the Chamber relied on numerous documents showing that Pusic ordered and approved releases. Volume 4, paragraph 1049. In particular, the evidence shows that Pusic was authorising and approving releases from the Heliodrom in the summer and autumn of 1993, according to a procedure that Pusic has set out in the decision of 12 August 1993 as head of the commission for HVO prisons and detention centres. Volume 4, paragraph 1158. And this procedure included - in addition to approval by Pusic - approval by the SIS, the HVO's information and security service; and the Department of Criminal Investigations of the military police; as well as guarantees that the detainees would leave the territory of Herceg-Bosna. I refer Your Honours, for example, to Exhibit P04450, P4686, P4799, P05094, and P5748. And Your Honours will find these exhibits in footnote 2172 of volume 4. The Chamber reasonably concluded also that Pusic's powers in organising releases increased in December 1993. Volume 4, paragraph 1050. In particular, following Mate Boban's 10 December decision to close the detention facilities, Pusic was involved in expulsions of Muslim detainees from Heliodrom, Gabela, and Ljubuski prison. The very same day, on 10 December 1993, Pusic proposed re-organisation of the work of the exchange commission and service. Exhibit P07102. This proposal included the task of "establishing the lists of persons who voluntarily want to leave the areas of the HR HB with the aim of reuniting the families." And here, of course, the meaning of "voluntarily" has to be interpreted in light of the coercive context. Pusic was also part of the working group established to implement Boban's decision. Volume 4, paragraph 1092. And the minutes of the working group session of 11 December reveal Pusic's attitude. "Mr. Pusic believes that they," that's the detainees, "should be released, but that at the same time all measures of organisation, protection, and security should be taken and, in particular, preparing the detainees so that they can be sent abroad." Exhibit P07148, page 5. And then a bit later: "Mr. Pusic believes that people over 50 years of age should be sent or, rather, handed over to the Muslims side on the left bank of the Neretva." That's Exhibit P07148, page 10. And the left bank, as Your Honours will recall, was besieged East Mostar, overcrowded and subject to heavy shelling and sniping. In the working group sessions two days later on 13 December, Mr. Ivica Lucic, the chief of the SIS, the HVO information and security service, presented some data. There are a total of 2.912 persons in five detention centres - and this included Heliodrom, Gabela, and Ljubuski - and of these persons, 1.238 will be transferred to the territory held by Muslim armed forces and 295 with proper documentation will be transferred to third countries. Exhibit P07143, page 4. So this was the plan, and the plan was followed through. And Pusic was involved in the execution by organising the expulsions of detainees from the Heliodrom, Gabela, and Ljubuski prison to ABiH-held territory, including East Mostar or third countries, sometimes from Heliodrom via Gabela prison. For example, on 13 December Pusic co-signs an order for release of 14 persons from the Heliodrom to the left bank, i.e., ABiH-held territory in besieged East Mostar. Exhibit P07141. Also on 13 December 1993, Pusic co-signs another order releasing 17 persons going to third countries, with a note that they were transferred from Ljubuski to Gabela on 15 December. Exhibit P07140. And I refer Your Honours to volume 4, paragraph 1160, in relation to the Heliodrom; para 1178 for Gabela; and 1183 for Ljubuski prison. As of late December 1993, numerous releases from the Heliodrom were carried out through exchanges. Volume 4, paragraph 1162. And again, Pusic - the head of the Service for Exchange of Detainees and Other Persons - was involved. In this context Pusic did not hesitate to keep some of the prisoners in detention for several months more when that allowed him to negotiate the release of HVO soldiers. Volume 4, paragraph 1166. For example, starting in mid-December 1993, Pusic ordered that a certain number of Muslims remain in detention in the Heliodrom in order to be used for exchanges. On 1 March 1994, the HVO, through Pusic, sent 121 Heliodrom detainees to Jablanica under ABiH control to be exchanged for 61 POW HVO members and 200 civilians. Volume 4, paragraph 1163. This shows that the exchanges were not limited to POWs but also included civilians. In this regard, I also refer Your Honours to Pusic's report of 31 March 1994, attachment 2. That's Exhibit P08136, pages 2 and 3. Although Boban took the decision to close detention centres on 10 December 1993, the last releases conducted through exchanges were organised by Pusic in April 1994. Volume 4, paragraph 1164. Pusic thus clearly contributed to the common plan through releases. Pusic also contributed to the common plan by being the link between the workings of the network of detention facilities and the most important members of the JCE. Volume 4, paragraph 1209. The Chamber based this, in particular, on Pusic regularly informing the HVO leadership about the progress of the implementation of Boban's 10 December decision. This finding is reasonable on the evidence, which shows that Pusic sent numerous reports about the implementation of this decision to, among others, the Herceg-Bosna government, the minister of defence, the military police administration, and the embassy of Croatia. Pusic reported twice on 15 December 1993, twice on 18 December, again on the 3rd of January, 1994. He also reported without explicit mention of Boban's decision on 24 February 1994, 2 March 1994, 31 March 1994, and 29 April 1994. And all reports are listed in footnotes 319 and 320 of the Prosecution response brief. For example, on 15 December 1993, Pusic sent the following report. We can see the date in the top left corner, and in the bottom right corner we see that Pusic sent the report as head of the exchange service. And Your Honours can see from the headings that the report relates to Ljubuski, Heliodrom, and Gabela. And I will take Your Honours through these three locations in more detail. It says the following has been done. In relation to Ljubuski: "14 persons were released from prison in Ljubuski and they will go to the left bank on their own will." This own will needs to be read in context, Your Honours. East Mostar remained under siege under intense shelling and sniping and was significantly overcrowded. "(2) 17 persons who will go to the third countries were released and they have necessary documents. "(3) Eight persons who will stay in HR HB in Citluk will go to third countries together with their family members. "Heliodrom. "(1) 57 persons who live in mixed marriages and have Croatian spouse were released from prison in Heliodrom. They will stay in the HR HB, whereas five persons want to go to the left bank because their families are there (expelled before). "(2) 12 Muslim women were released and they stayed on the right bank. "Gabela. "With mediation of the ICRC, 83 persons of Muslim ethnicity were released from Gabela. They were transferred to Split from where they will go to the third countries." Exhibit P07187. On 3 January 1994, Pusic reports that a total of 3.167 persons have been released. Of those, 1.935 were released to the left bank - besieged East Mostar - and area under the control of the ABiH; and 343 persons were -- 743, apologies, were released to third countries. Exhibit P07468. Your Honours, would this be an appropriate time for the break before I turn to the next contribution?
