utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to continue with the fourth contribution, namely, Pusic's contribution to the common plan by keeping persons detained who he knew were unlawfully detained and who were held in terrible conditions and were mistreated. Pusic was clearly aware that persons who -- were unlawfully detained. He made and received lists which indicated, from the age of the detainee or from their description as civilians, that they were not lawfully detained. As head of the Service for the Exchange of Prisoners or Other Persons, it was his task to set up a database on prisoners and other persons, Exhibit P03191. In particular, Pusic compiled lists of Heliodrom detainees on 15 September 1993 and received lists of Gabela and Ljubuski detainees. Volume 4, paragraphs 1135, 1171, 1172, and 1181. But Pusic did not release those detained civilians. Pusic was also clearly aware of terrible detention conditions, of overcrowding and mistreatment in detention. Through his role in the network of detention facilities, he had the power to do something about it but, for the most part, he did not. Rather, he contributed to the mistreatment by authorising or approving dangerous forced labour on the front line. Based on personal visits and reports he received, the Chamber reasonably concluded that Pusic knew of problems with the conditions of detention and of overcrowding in relation to Heliodrom and Ljubuski the entire time they functioned, volume 4, paragraph 1143 and 1182; in relation to Dretelj and Gabela from July 1993, volume 4, paragraph 1170; volume 3, paragraph 59; volume 4, paragraph 1176. And starting in July 1993, Pusic was also informed of mistreatment of detainees at the Heliodrom volume 4, paragraph 1145. This brings me to question 9 of Your Honours' preparation order. In question 9 Your Honours asked for the basis of the Chamber's finding in volume 4, paragraph 1056, that Pusic had the power to resolve problems related to conditions of confinement and mistreatment of detainees in the network of HVO detention centres. The answer is given in the same paragraph, notably Pusic's power to transfer detainees from one detention centre to another. In addition, the Chamber in this paragraph also relied on the power to release detainees. The relevant part of volume 4, paragraph 1056, says: "Berislav Pusic had a role and significant powers in the detention centres, notably the power to transfer detainees from one detention centre to another, to resolve problems related to conditions of confinement and mistreatment of detainees." This becomes even clearly maybe in the original French version of the judgement: [French spoken] [No interpretation] "... Berislav Pusic avait un rôle et des pouvoirs suffisamment importants dans les centres de détention, et notamment celui de transférer les détenus d'un centre de détention à un autre, pour remédier aux problèmes liés aux conditions de détention et aux mauvais traitements des personnes détenues." This reading is further confirmed by volume 4, paragraph 1143, as well as the Chamber's findings on Pusic's responsibility under JCE 1 in volume 4, paragraph 1203, where the Chamber noted that Pusic: "... never took the necessary measures to improve the conditions or to put a stop to the mistreatment such as moving the detainees to another detention centre or notifying the relevant authorities." Thus, Pusic could have improved the conditions in detention and alleviated the mistreatment by releasing and transferring detainees or by notifying the relevant authorities. Pusic had the power to do so. I have already discussed Pusic's power in relation to release. In addition, he could have transferred detainees. Pusic had the power to transfer detainees from one detention facility to another. In addition to the two pieces of evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber in volume 4, paragraph 1056, the record shows that Pusic on numerous occasions - either individually or jointly with others - ordered transfers of detainees between detention facilities. We have listed them in paragraph 51 of the Prosecution's response brief. In particular, the Chamber found in volume 4, paragraph 1182, that between May and September 1993 Pusic ordered the transfer of more than 100 detainees from Ljubuski prison to another detention facility. The evidence shows two transfers, one of 106 and one of 130 prisoners. That's Exhibit P2535 and P05083. The Chamber thus reasonably found Pusic could take action to transfer detainees. To challenge this conclusion the Defence has today in particular pointed to the fact that Pusic proposed transfer of detainees from the Heliodrom to Gabela due to overcrowding at the Heliodrom in January 1994. This proposal was rejected by Biskic, the deputy minister of defence for security and the military police of Herceg-Bosna. But, first of all, in testimony, Biskic explained the reasons he did not approve of this transfer. Namely, because they had established a company to provide security at the Heliodrom and that detainees should be exchanged from there. Transcript page 15130 and 15326. Moreover, Biskic only came to Herceg-Bosna on 8 November 1993 and only had contact with Pusic after Boban's 10 December order. Biskic blocking one of Pusic's attempt from moving detainees does not undermine Pusic's general ability to take measures to transfer detainees. Moreover, the evidence shows that prior to Biskic's arrival in Herceg-Bosna, Pusic did order the transfer of detainees. For example, on 6 November 1993 two detainees were transferred from Heliodrom to Gabela or order of Berislav Pusic. Exhibit P00352, page 31; and volume 1 of the judgement, paragraph 196. In addition, Pusic had the power to report to the authorities in charge of prisons, not only when he became part of the working group set up to inspect detention centres, but also as president of the commission for HVO prisons and detention centres. As president of the commission for HVO prisoners and detention centres, it was his formal responsibility to resolve problems relating to detention centres and prisons. Volume 1, paragraph 622. As the detention centres in the network were controlled by the military police administration, the HVO, or both, Pusic could have reported to Coric - the head of the MPA with whom he worked closely - or Pusic could have used his connections with other JCE members, such as Stojic, who ap pointed him as head of the commission on HVO prisons and detention centres, to report on the situation in HVO-run facilities. Despite his ability to take measures to improve detention conditions, Pusic failed to take action. Only in a few limited instances during his JCE membership, Pusic tried to improve conditions by suggesting to move people such as in January 1993 in the memorandum to Biskic or proposed new sites to hold detainees and to address overcrowding as part of delegation sent to Dretelj and Gabela in July 1993. This is clearly insufficient. Therefore, the Chamber reasonably found Pusic failed to take measures to address conditions of and mistreatment in detention. Volume 4, paragraph 1143, 1145, 1176, 1170, and 1182. Had Pusic raised issues in relation to detention facilities, he would have made the continuation of mistreatment more difficult. Those with powers over the detention centres would have been forced to either address Pusic's concern or remove Pusic from his role in the detention centre network or replace him. This would have disrupted the efficient implementation of the common criminal plan through the network of detention facilities. Pusic's failure to address prison conditions and mistreatment thus furthered the common criminal plan. To conclude on the contributions, Your Honours, on the basis of the totality of the evidence, there can be no doubt that Pusic's contributions taken cumulatively significantly contributed to the common plan. In particular, Pusic authorised and ordered highly dangerous forced labour, which forced Muslim detainees to agree to leave Herceg-Bosna and was a key player in implementing these expulsions of detainees. Grounds 1 and 6 of Pusic's appeal should be dismissed. This brings me to the last part of my submissions, namely, Pusic's shared intend, that is Ground 5. Pusic's conduct including the contributions I just described as well as his utterances show that he accepted all means necessary to ethnically the areas that Croats claimed, persecutions; forcible displacement, including to third countries; unlawful detention; cruel and inhumane treatment, including through detention conditions; killings and attacks and through forced labour; unlawful attack and terror; and destruction of Muslim property, including mosques. Deeply involved in detention matters, Pusic was clearly aware that they happened for a purpose. To displace Muslims from Herceg-Bosna with their families, including to third countries. Already in April 1993 Pusic knew about mass arrests. Volume 4, paragraph 1203. Pusic knew that terrible detention conditions, mistreatment during detention on forced labour were used to force detainees to agree to leave Herceg-Bosna and BiH if they were released. These Muslims had no real choice. They could either remain detained in extremely harsh conditions where they risked their life during dangerous forced labour or leave Herceg-Bosna. These displacements were not done for the security of the detainees or compelling military reasons. There were no measures in place for the return of detainees or their families. Quite the opposite. By destroying their houses, the HVO made sure they had nowhere to return to. Volume 3, paragraph 787. Pusic saw this in Sovici and Doljani. When Pusic entered Sovici and Doljani on 4 May 1993, together with Petkovic and other members of the delegation, Pusic saw that the villages were burned down. He saw that the men of working age and younger boys were held in harsh conditions, undernourished, and exhausted. One of the commission members, Hasan Rizvic talked about what the delegation saw in Sovici school: "We entered the school and what we saw was terrible. The people were exhausted and dirty." And then one line down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Goy, slow down a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Apologies. One line down he said: "They could not sleep without laying on their sides so that they would take up less space. Most started to cry, but still they told us they had not been mistreated. You could tell, however, that this was not true." Exhibit P10358, paragraph 40. And the Chamber's finding show he was right. Rizvic also explained that the delegation heard there were groups of women and children held in another hamlet. That's on paragraph 42 of Exhibit 10358. On the basis of this and other evidence, the Chamber reasonably concluded that Pusic was fully informed about the arrest and detention of the population of the villages. He knew of detention of civilians and of the harsh detention conditions, was aware of the destruction of Muslim property and the mosques. He also knew of the displacement of the detainees from Sovici and Doljani the next day. Nevertheless, Pusic continued to carry out his functions within the HVO. Volume 4, paragraphs 1102, 1104. Pusic was aware not only of the detention but also of the horrific conditions, that they were a necessary means to achieve the expulsion, but he failed to take necessary measures to improve the conditions or report the mistreatment. Rather, he tried to conceal and hide HVO responsibility. Volume 4, paragraph 1201. At a meeting organised by ECMM representatives on 16 June 1993, Pusic and Coric denied the information reported to them regarding evictions of Muslims from West Mostar to East Mostar. They told ECMM that the evictions never happened, and if they had, there were the acts of criminals over whom the HVO had no control. Volume 4, paragraph 1198. Pusic's intent is also shown in a comment he made in September 1993 in relation to the situation in Mostar. Pusic said the only suitable solution was to "send all the Muslims from West Herzegovina to East Mostar where they come from." Volume 4, paragraph 1115. If we could move into private session for just one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's move into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Ms. Goy. And slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Yes, apologies. In addition, as I already mentioned, in the meeting of 11 December 1993 to implement Boban's 10 December decision, Pusic insisted on the fact that all the detainees should be sent abroad. In the working group meeting two days later, on 13 December 1993, Pusic continued to assert that Muslim detainees needed to be sent to third countries. Volume 4, paragraph 1128. In light of these statements, his key role in detention matters and his failure to improve the conditions and his attempt to hide HVO responsibility, it was reasonable for the Chamber to infer that Pusic not only shared the intent for unlawful detention and horrible conditions and mistreatment, the destruction of property and of mosques, but also for the displacement itself that he shared the discriminatory intent for persecution. Pusic's disrespect for human life and his willingness to accept whatever means it takes to implement the plan becomes clear when one looks at how Pusic behaved during the siege of East Mostar. Pusic had his office in West Mostar and was therefore aware from the beginning what was happening. Prior to the siege, Pusic was not only aware of arrest and detention of Muslims from West Mostar, he took part in the arrest campaign in May 1993 and in the operation to remove Muslims from West Mostar to East Mostar. Volume 4, paragraphs 1110 and 1111. And as I already mentioned, he tried to conceal these evictions and denied them in the meeting with the ECMM on 16 June 1993. With his office in West Mostar, Pusic would have been aware of the suffering of the civilian population trapped in East Mostar, of the shelling and sniping and terror. How would someone react who did not share the intent for the crimes forming part of the siege? One would expect that this person would use the means at his or her disposal to protest against this behaviour and try to help the trapped Muslims. And what did Pusic do? Rather than protesting, Pusic hindered, even paralysed humanitarian evacuations. Rather than assisting the people trapped in East Mostar, Pusic made living conditions worse. Volume 4, paragraph 1122. Pusic participated in negotiations with representatives of international organisations but showed little willingness to co-operate. He made negotiations difficult, insisted on special evacuation permits. For one Muslim to be evacuated from East Mostar, a Croat had to be moved from a besieged enclave. Volume 4, paragraph 1121. This shows that Pusic was committed to the common purpose, that he accepted and shared the intent for the types of crimes committed in East Mostar to achieve Croat domination. Murder, unlawful attack, and terror. This attitude is in line with Pusic's continued approval for forced labour even after he was on notice that some detainees had not returned from their assignments on the front line. Volume 4, paragraph 1151. Pusic not only shared the intent for unlawful forced labour but also for killings during forced labour assignments. On the totality of Pusic's conduct, the Chamber's finding is therefore reasonable, that Pusic shared the intent for the common purpose crimes. Ground 5 should be dismissed. Let me end my submissions with an answer to Your Honours' question number 4 about the impact of the reversal of the finding of murder and wilful killing in relation to the killing of civilians in Enver Sljivo's house in Dusa. Ms. Gustafson explained last week in the Prosecutions response to Prlic's appeal that this would not change the scope of the common purpose nor the shared intent of Mr. Pusic. That's at questions 4(a) and (b). As regards question 4(c), Your Honours will recall that Pusic is not convicted under JCE 3 for murder and wilful killing, so this question technically relates to the Prosecution appeal but since counsel for Mr. Pusic raised it today, I will also respond today. If a finding on murder and wilful killing in relation to the attack on Enver Sljivo's house were overturned, this would not impact Pusic's liability under JCE 3 as alleged in the Prosecution's appeal. Pusic was not a JCE member at the time of the Gornji Vakuf attack in January 1993. He only joined in April 1993. In the appeal, the Prosecution therefore has not relied on Pusic's knowledge regarding specific events in Gornji Vakuf in support of the appeal. To conclude, Your Honours, on the basis of the totality of the evidence, the Chamber's conclusions are reasonable. Pusic was a JCE member who significantly contributed and shared the intent for the common purpose crimes. His appeal should be dismissed. Unless Your Honours have any questions, this ends the Prosecution's submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I, first of all, thank you for the time. I don't propose to, nor is it possible for me to, reply to every argument that's been advanced this morning by the Prosecutor, particularly when the reply of the Prosecution, in my respectful submission, has in large parts consisted of a resuscitation or regurgitation of passages from the Trial Chamber's findings. These have been repeated uncritically. We have our arguments, our position is clear from our appeal brief, and I hope from what I've said this morning, one of our main concerns remains that the arguments that we've advanced in our appeal brief have not been engaged with and directly addressed by the Trial Chamber, a Chamber that only dedicated a few pages in its many thousands of pages of findings to Mr. Pusic. So, Your Honour, if there are any points that I haven't addressed that were raised this morning, by no means does that mean that we accept or concede anything. And, Your Honours, I'll start with this reply by just looking at -- I'm going to focus on question 4 and the issue of forced labour, I'm deliberately focusing on that because, really, in my opinion, that's the most serious allegation against Mr. Pusic. That is the most grave crime that he is alleged to have a direct input in. And, Your Honour, what I said this morning is there is, in my submission, some confusion in the Trial Chamber's reasoning, there is -- I don't have the references at hand, they were referred to this morning. At one point the Chamber talks of significant powers that Mr. Pusic had to order forced labour assignments. In other parts of the judgement there is reference to substantial powers. So there is something of a muddle there, and I was wondering if Prosecution this morning would be able to sort of -- or to assist us in determining what the position was, is it the case of significant powers, is it the case of substantial powers, and I'm not entirely clear that the picture -- well, I think it remains just as opaque as it was before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Pocar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. You mentioned this morning even before, significant substantial powers in the difference. Can you give us a couple of examples where the substantial is mentioned in the text in the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think what I'm alluding to is a general conclusion, and I will put my finger on it at some point, that Mr. Pusic, in opinion of the Chamber, had substantial powers over the network of detention facilities, which I would assume is a finding that incorporates his powers over forced labour. And the finding at paragraph 104 -- sorry, 1203, at volume 4, that he also played a significant role in the use of Heliodrom detainees, sending them on forced labour assignments, that's paragraph 1203. And I think it is implicit from what is said with references to orders and the general context and tenor of the Chamber's findings in the relation to his powers over detention centres in general, that some confusion arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I think the problem is that the Trial Chamber never really nails its colours to the mast as to what Mr. Pusic's powers are and what the source of those powers are. So in my mind, and perhaps you share this confusion, it is not entirely clear whether they're saying that he played a significant role or he had substantial powers. Although they use the word "significant" in paragraph 1203, when one looks at the general tenor and context of the findings on detention centres, it seems as if the Trial Chamber's conclusion is that he had substantial powers when it came to the HVO network of detention centres. And, Your Honour, I say that because one can contrast the Chamber's findings on detention centres and separate those with the other crimes on the indictment, if you look at prisoner releases, exchanges, humanitarian evacuations, it is quite clear that in respect of those areas, the Chamber has found that that Mr. Pusic had significant powers. But under the umbrella heading of detention centres it uses and is more prepared to use the word "substantial powers." So I'm not entirely -- I hope that assists. I have been also passed references to the following paragraphs, I don't have the ability to look at themselves on my feet, but if I can cite these to you now, they're all in volume 4. utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, it's on the basis of these rather muddled and confusing at times findings that ... May I have just a minute, Your Honours, just to resume as to where I left off. Well, Your Honours, it's on the basis of what we say this rather muddled analysis that nonetheless the Chamber comes to the conclusion that it does, that Mr. Pusic made a significant contribution to the JCE; and it finds that he made a significant contribution in respect of forced labour. The allegations relevant to forced labour not on the basis of -- only on the basis of what he did, i.e., these orders that we dispute but also on the basis of his omissions to act, i.e., his acceptance in the general context. And what concerns us is that the evidence is so unclear, we would say, that it really prohibits any finding beyond reasonable doubt in respect of this particular area. And we have already highlighted our concerns in respect of Mr. Pusic's position within the HVO hierarchy. Can I just directly address some of the documents that were produced this morning by the Prosecution as further evidence that he could give orders. There were two of the documents that were adduced this morning. The first is P3583, and this was referred to as a general order from Mr. Pusic. Your Honours, we would ask you to examine this document, apply what we called our handle-with-care warning. This is again a document not signed by Mr. Pusic. There is endorsed on it in writing by a member of the Heliodrom staff the words as "per the general order by Mr. Pusic," and it's a document that refers to a request, a request made on the 20th of July, 1993, for 15 prisoners to be taken out to perform work. And that's a request made by Mile Pulik [phoen] who is the HVO Mostar battalion commander. So what was said this morning is that we, the Defence, were incorrect in saying that the only evidence of any orders or approvals emanated from Mr. Josip Praljak. What we should have said, perhaps just to clarify, is that the only witness who gave evidence of these orders was Mr. Josip Praljak. However, the documents are indeed endorsed by other individuals which include other staff at the Heliodrom. But I think the basic thrust of our submission, which is that these are not orders. They're notes of conversations where the endorsements are written by either Mr. Praljak in the main - Josip Praljak, that is - or by other staff at the Heliodrom and they should not be construed as evidence of any powers that Mr. Pusic has. And we would make the same submission again in regards to I think a think a reference that you were shown to a document. I don't have it at hand, but there was a reference to 700 detainees in total, a schedule. And that was taken from the Heliodrom log-book. In that log-book it would appear that endorsements were made as approved by Mr. Pusic and in the hand of whoever was making entries into the log-book at the time, and that may or may not have been Mr. Josip Praljak. So if we could clarify that, but our position remains as -- you're well aware that those documents do not provide the foundation for a finding beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Pusic had the power to issue orders for detainees to be taken out on forced labour assignments. Your Honours, it's interesting and we've said again this morning that those orders, we say, have to be read against the general context which is that as conceded by the Prosecution this morning, that the Chamber cannot precisely specify the source of Mr. Pusic's powers when it comes to this issue of forced labour. We would apply that perhaps more generally. It can't precisely satisfy the source of his powers in respect of any activities that he is said to have engaged in. What was also said this morning is that it wasn't important and what seemed to be implied is that it didn't really matter whether he had de jure powers or not; we should consider the evidence of his de facto powers in this area. And it was also said by the Prosecution this morning that it didn't really matter whether we could make a firm finding as to whether he had any subordinates because he wasn't -- or this isn't a case where we're considering his 7(3) liability. We're looking at his liability as a member of the JCE, and all that needs to be proved there is that he made a significant contribution. That contribution can be made on the basis of not just his acts but also his omissions to act if they constitute acceptance. What remains troubling for us is that - again, as I've said earlier today - the evidence of or the evidence that these conclusions as to his influence and powers are drawn from are -- well, the evidence is so unclear, it's so conflicting, it's so contradictory. How can it support any findings beyond reasonable doubt? That is the question that we advance. Your Honours, I would refer you to paragraph 25 of our appeal brief. In that paragraph, we talk about the Pusic paradox and what we say is that it's because of this -- these multiple failures on the part of the Trial Chamber. Their failure to specify who his subordinates are, their failure to specify - as the Prosecution conceded this morning - what the precise source of his power is. It's because of those failures there remains a conundrum. There remain an uncertainty as to the exact ambit of Mr. Pusic's powers and influence. And there must remain some concern as to whether the Chamber properly applied the burden of proof when making their findings. And that, Your Honours, really is in summary the thrust of our submissions when it comes to this particular issue of forced labour. So we say that this paradox, the Pusic paradox we call it, we also say that applies more generally to all the findings in the Trial Chamber's judgement in respect of all the other areas of activity that he was involved in. Your Honours, in response to what was said this morning in regards to detention centres and the conditions of detention, there was no reference in the narrative you heard in the first part of the Prosecution's submissions to Mr. Pusic having any role in the setting up of the network of detention centres. And you know from the Trial Chamber's judgement that he is not said to have joined the JCE until April 1993. Your Honour, in respect of his role before the 10th of December, 1993, as regards detention centres, we -- we're not going to add anything to what we've already addressed you on this morning and what's in our appeal brief. I would like to address you on what was said about Mr. Pusic's role in detention centres, in releases, in exchanges after the 10th of December. In particular what was said this morning about the role of Marjan Biskic role. And, Your Honours, I think the Prosecution referred to the fact that he was posted -- parachuted in I said this morning from Croatia in November 1993, remained in situ working with the HVO HZ HB until 1994. And, Your Honours, central to our case is his assessment that Mr. Pusic could not give orders to him or anyone else. And we say that analysis which directly applies to this question of detention centres - that was the area that he was intimately involved with - directly contradicts the account that you heard this morning from the Prosecution of Mr. Pusic's powers increasing. His powers increased after the 10th of December, 1993, a phrase that was repeated many times and is taken verbatim from the Trial Chamber's judgement. His powers were such that he was somebody who played a key role in organising the exchanges and releases of detainees after that date. Well, how does that square with Mr. Biskic's assessment? It doesn't. And, Your Honours, how does it square with the failure of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to identify Mr. Pusic's subordinates and to identify his source of power? We say that same paradox applies in relation to detention centres. Turning now to releases. Our case is as set out in the appeal brief. We say Mr. Pusic had no unilateral power to order the release of prisoners, their exchange, or their transfer. In reference to prisoner releases specifically, you heard this morning reference to Mr. Pusic describing the procedure that had to be followed before a detainee could be released. Reference would have to be made to other departments within the HVO, to the security department known as the SIS, also to the criminal investigation department known as the CID. So, Your Honours, what I would say the narrative and account that you were presented this morning really oversimplifies the position when it comes to releases and exchanges. Whatever happened in respect to those that were detained in the HVO network of detention centres, if they remained in detention, if they were sent to third countries, if they were released to ABiH territory, if they were forced to stay in their homes or to stay in Mostar when there was a conflict going on, whatever happened we say the evidence does not show that Mr. Pusic had the power to influence or dictate their fate. When it comes to the one-for-one or all-for-all exchange policies, again we say that Mr. Pusic did not have the power to determine these issues so we say the evidence does not show that Mr. Pusic had the power to determine these issues. And so, Your Honour, we say that's not a black-and-white issue as you may have had the impression from what you've heard this morning. There was also, Your Honours, reference to the decision in Kvocka this morning alluded by my learned friend for the Prosecution. What I would say here is that in contrast in distinguishing that particular case, the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber didn't find that Mr. Pusic was just a clerk or administrator; that's not what the import of the Trial Chamber's findings are. It's also not said by the Trial Chamber or by the Prosecution that Mr. Pusic was just a link between the leadership and what happened on the ground. And, Your Honour, it's -- we would suggest that the evidence would not even support a conviction for Mr. Pusic if it were the case that he was just shown to be a clerk or administrative officer. We would still maintain the position that that finding would not support the conclusion that he made a significant contribution to the JCE. So, Your Honour, I'm just going to end quickly. I think we would ask the Chamber to look at the evidence regarding Mr. Pusic's conduct in totality, not to view elements of it in isolation, not to bifurcate in the way the Trial Chamber has evidence about detention centres, separate that from evidence concerning the activities of Mr. Pusic in the areas of prisoner exchange, in the areas of humanitarian evacuation releases and transfers. We'll ask you to take a global approach in this case. And in response directly to what was said this morning, we would consider that the Prosecution are really at times asking and expecting the impossible of Mr. Pusic on the ground. Judging him by today's standards, it was said that -- or it was directly raised the question of why he -- why did he not protest? Why did he not report some of the atrocities that he must have known about? Well, Your Honour, this is a criminal trial. It's the Prosecution's burden to prove beyond reasonable doubt; it's the Trial Chamber's obligation to find that evidences that has been brought to show beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Pusic is guilty. And, Your Honours, our concerns about this judgement really rest upon the fact that what remains unclear, what remains opaque is the question of exactly what subordinates Mr. Pusic had, what the extent of his power was, what his ability was to influence events. And that, Your Honour, are questions that remain -- the answers to those questions remain unclear, despite what you've heard this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sahota. That brings us to the end of today's session. Tomorrow we have a long day, as you know. The submissions will be followed by any statement that each one of the appellants may wish to make. I would suggest that -- to counsel that if any one of the appellants doesn't wish or does not intend to make a statement to let us know so that we can make the necessary arrangements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of March, 2017, at 9.00 a.m.
